title: Epigenetic pioneering by SWI/SNF family remodelers
abstract: In eukaryotic genomes, transcriptional machinery and nucleosomes compete for binding to DNA sequences; thus, a crucial aspect of gene regulatory element function is to modulate chromatin accessibility for transcription factor (TF) and RNA polymerase binding. Recent structural studies have revealed multiple modes of TF engagement with nucleosomes, but how initial "pioneering" results in steady-state DNA accessibility for further TF binding and RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) engagement has been unclear. Even less well understood is how distant sites of open chromatin interact with one another, such as when developmental enhancers activate promoters to release RNAPII for productive elongation. Here, we review evidence for the centrality of the conserved SWI/SNF family of nucleosome remodeling complexes, both in pioneering and in mediating enhancer-promoter contacts. Consideration of the nucleosome unwrapping and ATP hydrolysis activities of SWI/SNF complexes, together with their architectural features, may reconcile steady-state TF occupancy with rapid TF dynamics observed by live imaging.

narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

This Molecular Cell article has accumulated 73 OpenAlex citations and sits in the top 10% of its field and year, indicating strong early scholarly uptake. Its influence is broadening through downstream reuse in 74 works, including articles, preprints, reviews, and book chapters, with the citing literature clustered around chromatin dynamics, remodeling, epigenetics, and cancer-related gene regulation.

Full narrative

Kami Ahmad, Sandipan Brahma, and Steven Henikoff’s 2023 study addresses a central problem in gene regulation: how SWI/SNF-family remodelers help convert nucleosome-occluded DNA into accessible regulatory elements for transcription factor and RNA polymerase II engagement. Published in Molecular Cell, the article has already been cited 73 times, placing it in the top 10% of papers in its field and publication year and suggesting that it has become an important reference point for ongoing work on chromatin accessibility and pioneer activity.

The citation landscape shows that the paper is being used not only in primary research but also in synthesis. Of the documented downstream reuse, most is in research articles, with additional uptake in preprints, reviews, and book chapters. The most common themes in citing work are genomics and chromatin dynamics, chromatin remodeling and cancer, and epigenetics and DNA methylation, which together point to a broad conceptual reach across mechanism-focused and disease-oriented studies.

The work is also visible in the more immediate preprint ecosystem, with bioRxiv among the top citing venues and a substantial share of citing outputs appearing before formal journal publication. That pattern is consistent with a paper that is helping shape a fast-moving area of chromatin biology, where researchers are actively testing how remodeler activity interfaces with pioneer factors, enhancer function, promoter accessibility, and transcriptional control.

Evidence of interpretive uptake is also present in scite: most citation statements are neutral mentions, with a small number of supporting citations and one contradicting statement, indicating that the paper is being actively engaged rather than simply repeated. The broader record also shows documented dataset citation activity and two open repository instances, while formal public-discourse signals are limited in the available archive. Overall, the article appears to be establishing itself as a durable mechanistic reference in the SWI/SNF and chromatin-remodeling literature, with influence extending from basic chromatin biology into cancer and epigenetics research.
